newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy court rejects bid to change voting system.
newsitem.headline: Italy court rejects bid to change voting system.

text.p: Italy's Constitutional Court on Thursday rejected a request for a referendum to scrap a proportional representation part of the country's electoral system, but gave the go-ahead to 11 other votes later this year.

The proportional representation proposal, put forward by the radical Reformist party of veteran civil rights campaigner Marco Pannella, sought to abolish the electoral system under which 25 percent of seats in parliament are selected.
It was the second time in two years that the Court had thrown out such a bid, which would have been a bombshell for the system. A similar attempt was declared unconstitutional in 1995.

The Court's decision came after three weeks of deliberation on whether to allow 30 proposed referendums, on issues ranging from advertising to drugs, hunting and ways of limiting the power of central government.

The record number of referendum proposals has sparked heated political debate on whether the mechanism -- used in 1974 in a landmark plebiscite to approve divorce -- is being abused to override parliamentary law-making.
The Court gave the green light to 11 of the proposed referendums, but rejected 19.
Among those allowed was one seeking to abolish the use of "golden shares" that give the Treasury special powers in privatised companies deemed to be of public interest.
Another proposing restrictions on the state's powers over regional governments was accepted but a proposed referendum to liberalise soft drugs was thrown out.
Italians voted in 1995 in 12 referendums. The latest batch will all go to the people on the same Sunday between mid-April and mid-June. The date will be set by President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro.
Fifty percent of the electorate has to vote for the process to be valid and opponents have already begun lobbying for voters to stay at home.

Italy's electoral law was itself amended after a referendum in 1993 that showed overwhelming support for a change from pure proportional representation following the massive corruption scandals that toppled the country's old political guard.
The system was amended to a mix of 75 percent majority voting and 25 percent proportional representation.

Other referendum proposals vetoed by the Court included moves to demilitarise the finance police, to slash the amount of advertising on state broadcaster RAI and to abolish the Tourism and Industry ministries.
